## Conclusions
**The set** (`scripts/build_grouped_val_set.py`, 4 folds x 300 reserved images): every image shows 2+ objects of one
category, with RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg expressions merged per object. Its statistics match the LPCVC sample
closely: 4.1 GT captions/img (sample 4.1), 4.7 words/caption (sample 5.0); about 7.6 other same-category images per
image in a fold.

**Paired deltas** (`paired_deltas.json`, mean [95% CI], points):

| Comparison | grouped | RefCOCOg-LPCVC | LPCVC sample |
|---|---|---|---|
| official baseline -> B FT (010) | +28.4 [+26.6, +30.2] | +24.1 | +4.0 [+1.6, +6.9] |
| B pretrained -> B FT on RefCOCO family (010) | **+22.0** | +16.0 | **+2.2** [+0.4, +4.2] |
| B pretrained -> B FT on COCO Captions (020) | **+4.6** | +4.3 | **+1.8** [+0.4, +3.9] |
| B FT (010) -> S3 FT (017) | -0.5 [-1.5, +0.6] | +0.7 [-0.3, +1.8] | +1.5 [-0.4, +3.7] |
| B FT (010) -> distilled (012) | -7.2 | -5.4 | +0.5 [-0.6, +1.8] |
| B pretrained -> S3 pretrained | +0.8 [-0.0, +1.6] | +0.8 [+0.1, +1.5] | +0.2 |

Model ranking (12 models): Spearman 0.99 grouped vs RefCOCOg-LPCVC, 0.89 grouped vs sample, 0.91 RefCOCOg vs sample.

**Pool-size control** (`pool56.json`, `scripts/subsample_pool.py`): random 56-image subsets, so the candidate pool
is about the sample's size (grouped 229 captions vs the sample's 211):

| Model | grouped@56 | RefCOCOg@56 | sample (56) |
|---|---|---|---|
| official baseline | 73.9 | 85.5 | 87.4 |
| B pretrained | 78.6 | 89.4 | 89.2 |
| B FT RefCOCO (010) | 92.0 | 98.0 | 91.4 |
| B FT COCO Captions (020) | 81.9 | 91.9 | 91.0 |

**What we learned.**
1. Pool size explains only part of the score gap. At a matched pool, the baseline still scores 73.9 on grouped vs 87.4
   on the sample. LPCVC images are easier: salient, mostly distinct categories, clean captions. Our COCO images are
   cluttered, with small objects and noisy crowd-sourced captions ("Cat number 2", typos, all caps).
2. The grouped set ranks models like the other two sets. It is harder and far from ceiling (best 68%), so it separates
   models the sample cannot.
3. **It does not remove the caption-style bias. It makes the bias clearer.** Training on COCO Captions gives about
   the same gain everywhere (+4.6 / +4.3 / +1.8, all significant). Training on RefCOCO-family captions gives a gain 10x
   larger on the two RefCOCO-family sets than on the sample (+22 / +16 vs +2.2). Most of the validation gain from
   fine-tuning is learning RefCOCO's annotation style, which LPCVC does not share. The real LPCVC gain we can claim
   is the sample's: +2.2 over B pretrained and +4.0 over the official baseline, both significant.
4. Decisions that depend on the training-caption source (RefCOCO vs COCO, distillation from a general teacher) cannot be
   made on RefCOCO-family validation. On the sample, 010, 012, 013, 017 and 020 are all within noise of each other.
   Comparisons between models trained on the same data (compression variants, students) should be mostly
   unaffected, because the bias is shared. Example: S3 vs B gives the same small gap pretrained, fine-tuned, and on
   every set.

**Decision.** Report all three sets. Use grouped + RefCOCOg-LPCVC to rank variants trained on the same data. Do not
claim the +16 validation gain as an LPCVC gain. The next soundness step is an **out-of-family** LPCVC-like set, with
captions not written by RefCOCO annotators: either Visual Genome attribute annotations on non-COCO (Flickr) images
("The <attribute> <object>" for 2+ same-name objects), or ~100 images hand-captioned by the team in the LPCVC style.
